newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FEATURE-Colourful past no blessing for Jardines.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Colourful past no blessing for Jardines.

text.p: The oversize port-holes at the apex of Jardine House provide Alasdair Morrison with a sweeping vista of modern Hong Kong across the world's busiest harbour to the dragon-back ridge of hills guarding China.
Outside his wood-panelled office hangs a portrait of the 19th century Chinese mandarin Howqua in splendid silken robes.

Howqua's collaboration a century and a half ago with two buccaneering Scottish adventurers, William Jardine and James Matheson, made him reputedly the world's richest man. His fortune was estimated at $26 million in dollars of the day, much of it stashed in Baring Brothers' Bank in London.
STEEPED IN HONG KONG HISTORY

For Morrison, managing director of Jardine Matheson at the historic moment when Hong Kong reverts to China, the company's colourful past, so intimately entwined with the colonisation of Hong Kong, can be as much a curse as a blessing.
Jardine and Matheson are names synonymous with the opium trade which led to war between Britain and China and resulted in the British seizing Hong Kong at gunpoint in 1841.
"For a company like us, inevitably there is a lot of preoccupation about what impact the handover of sovereignty is going to have," he told Reuters in a recent interview.

"But I can honestly say we feel very confident in the future," he said, "and that the future Hong Kong government will maintain Hong Kong's level business playing field, the integrity of the (commercial) system."
A FINGER IN MANY HONG KONG PIES

Jardine's directors no longer sit on the legislature, and it no longer dominates Hong Kong's economy. There is lots of homegrown and international competition, including now from mainland Chinese companies.
But it is virtually impossible to spend more than a day or so here without somehow swelling the Jardine Matheson coffers.
It is Hong Kong's largest landlord in the downtown financial district, with five million sq feet (450,000 sq metres) of prime office space in the world's most expensive real estate market.
The cream of label-conscious Hong Kong's classiest stores -- Tiffany's, Gucci and Vuitton -- operate from a Jardine mall.

It owns the cluster of buildings housing the Hong Kong stock exchange. The Mandarin Oriental Hotel, regularly voted the world's best, is part of the Jardines stable. It holds half of Hong Kong's largest merchant bank, Jardine Fleming.
It sells the ubiquitous Mercedes Benz limousines which clog Hong Kong streets, Ikea furniture from Sweden and groceries through its Wellcome supermarket chain.
Want a late-night snack? The Seven 11 convenience store chain is part of the Jardine empire. Call from a public phone and a Jardine employee will probably collect the coins.
Jardine Matheson is the biggest private-sector employer in the ultra-modern city Morrison views from his skyscraper office.
Its commercial tentacles stretch to 30 countries in Europe, North America and throughout Australasia.
Morrison's preoccupations are those of any tycoon running a large conglomerate as the 21st century dawns.

Yet nearly every time Jardine Matheson acts, someone somewhere dredges up its connection with China's humiliation in the opium wars and concludes that the July 1 Hong Kong handover spells trouble for one of the last of the British Hongs.
BACK TO ITS ROOTS
It has been a rocky countdown for Jardine Matheson. Yet for all the ups and downs of the past decade, Jardines is once again expanding back into the China trade where it began.
Jardines risked invoking Beijing's wrath when it shifted its domicile from Hong Kong to Bermuda in 1984.
The move came with the ink barely dry from the initialling of the Sino-British Joint Declaration fixing the 1997 handover.
But 70 percent of Hong Kong's larger companies followed suit, including ones run by pro-Beijing entrepreneurs named by China to the post-colonial bodies responsible for Hong Kong's future.

The delisting of the Jardine group's companies from the Hong Kong stock exchange in 1994 and 1995 was viewed by China as a case of rats deserting a sinking ship, although Jardines' board clearly stated that its disagreement with Hong Kong stock market listing regulations was its sole reason for going elsewhere.
When Beijing objected to a contract awarded to a consortium led by Jardines to develop the territory's ninth containner terminal, it referred to Jardines' link with the opium wars.
Yet China eventually approved the port project last September after a face-saving reshuffle of its participants.

In early May, just eight weeks before the handover, Jardine chairman Henry Keswick and Morrison were toasted in Beijing by Chinese Vice-Premier Zhu Rongji and the top Chinese official in charge of Hong Kong policy, Lu Ping.

Jardines now operates more than 70 joint ventures in China, employing more than 15,000 and generating a turnover of more than US$1 billion and is seeking to sink its roots deeper by acquiring a major commercial property in Beijing, Morrison said.
Morrison, like Jardine Matheson itself, has no plans to pack his bags and leave the place he made his home 26 years ago.
"There is something special about Hong Kong, not always easy to define, but which is recognised by everyone who has visited the territory," he said.
